title: Vector Databases: Indexing, ANN Search & Production Patterns — Audio Guide

chapters.title: Mental Model
chapters.script: Think of a vector database as a deliberate trade-off: you intentionally give up exactness to gain speed, and you make that trade-off adjustable. Exact nearest neighbor search over millions of high-dimensional vectors requires scanning every vector, which simply does not work at scale. So every vector database is fundamentally an approximate nearest neighbor index, one that accepts almost the right neighbors in exchange for sub-linear query time. You get a knob that slides between recall and latency, like the ef parameter in HNSW or nprobe in IVF. A vector database is not just a database that happens to hold embeddings; it is an approximate nearest neighbor index with durability, metadata filtering, and operational features bolted on. This reframes every design decision as asking where you are on the recall-latency-cost surface and what moves you. Your choice of index sets the baseline; quantization buys memory at a recall cost; metadata filtering interacts with graph traversal in ways you might not expect. This storage layer sits beneath retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, and recommendations. The vectors come from embedding models, and how you split your documents determines the number and quality of vectors your database must index and search.

chapters.title: The Nearest Neighbor Problem
chapters.script: At its core, a vector database solves the nearest neighbor problem. Given a query vector and a collection of N vectors, you want the k vectors most similar to the query. Exact nearest neighbor search computes similarity between the query and every vector, which is order N times d operations for N vectors of dimension d. That becomes prohibitive at scale. Scanning one hundred million 768-dimensional vectors requires roughly three hundred billion floating-point operations per query. Approximate nearest neighbor algorithms trade a small amount of accuracy for orders-of-magnitude speedup. They typically achieve ninety-five to ninety-nine percent recall, meaning they find that fraction of the true nearest neighbors, while delivering sub-millisecond latency on millions of vectors.

chapters.title: ANN Core Primitives
chapters.script:
Now, about HNSW.

Hierarchical Navigable Small World, or HNSW, is the most widely deployed approximate nearest neighbor algorithm. It is the default index in Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector. HNSW constructs a multi-layer graph where each node is a vector and edges connect similar vectors. During construction, vectors are inserted one at a time. Each vector gets a random maximum layer, following an exponential distribution: most vectors appear only in the bottom layer, layer zero, while few reach higher layers. At each layer the algorithm performs a greedy search to find the nearest existing nodes, then creates bidirectional edges to the M closest neighbors. When you search, you start from a fixed entry point at the highest layer and run greedy search there, then descend to the next layer at the local minimum. At layer zero, the densest layer, you perform a more thorough beam search with a configurable efSearch parameter that controls the search width. Key parameters include M, the maximum connections per node, typically sixteen to sixty-four; efConstruction, the beam width during construction, typically 128 to 512; and efSearch, the beam width during search, which you can tune at query time. HNSW gives excellent recall-latency characteristics, often above ninety-five percent recall at sub-millisecond latency for million-scale datasets. The main disadvantage is memory consumption: the graph structure requires about one kilobyte per vector beyond the vector data itself. For one hundred million vectors at 768 dimensions, expect around four hundred gigabytes total memory, three hundred of which is for the vectors and one hundred for the graph.

Now, about IVF.

The Inverted File Index, or IVF, partitions the vector space into clusters using k-means, then searches only the nearest clusters at query time. During construction you run k-means clustering to create nlist centroids, typically between the square root of N and four times the square root of N. Each vector is assigned to its nearest centroid, creating an inverted list per cluster. At search time you compute distances from the query to all centroids, select the nprobe nearest clusters, then exhaustively scan all vectors within those clusters. The key trade-off is that IVF is more memory-efficient than HNSW because there is no graph overhead, and it allows disk-based storage of inverted lists. However, it requires a training step, and recall can degrade with skewed data distributions. At the same recall level, HNSW typically achieves lower latency.

Now, about Product Quantization.

Product quantization, or PQ, compresses vectors by splitting each vector into subvectors and quantizing each subvector independently. This gives you both memory reduction and fast distance computation using lookup tables. For example, you split a 768-dimensional vector into ninety-six subvectors of eight dimensions each. For each subgroup you train a codebook of 256 centroids, using one byte per subvector. The compressed representation is then ninety-six bytes instead of 3072 bytes, a thirty-two times compression. Distance computation is done by pre-computing distances from the query subvectors to all centroids in each codebook, producing 24,576 table lookups. You then approximate the full distance using table lookups and additions, which is dramatically faster than computing actual float distances. The most common production configuration combines IVF for coarse partitioning with PQ for compression within each partition, enabling billion-scale search with manageable memory. The trade-off is that PQ introduces quantization error, reducing recall compared to exact representations. The error is controlled by the number of subquantizers: more subquantizers give better accuracy but more memory. Typically PQ adds two to five percent recall loss but enables ten to thirty times memory reduction.

chapters.title: Vector Database Comparison
chapters.script:
When you choose a vector database, you weigh operational model, performance, and features. Pinecone is fully managed and serverless as of 2024. Its vectors are stored in distributed pods with automatic sharding and replication, and the serverless architecture bills per query and storage rather than per pod-hour. Pinecone gives zero operational overhead and consistent performance, with built-in metadata filtering and namespaces for multi-tenancy. But it is proprietary with no self-hosting option, and you have limited control over indexing parameters. It works best for teams wanting managed infrastructure at moderate scale, up to low billions of vectors.

Weaviate is open source, written in Go, and uses HNSW indexing with dynamic updates. It has a unique modules system for built-in vectorization that can call embedding APIs automatically. It supports multi-modal data, GraphQL, and hybrid search with BM25 and vector built in. Its limitations include HNSW-only indexing, which can be memory-intensive at large scale, cluster management complexity, and a Go codebase that limits community contributions from the Python-dominant ML community.

Qdrant is open source, written in Rust. It uses a custom HNSW implementation with modifications for filtered search and supports on-disk storage with memory-mapped vectors. Qdrant offers excellent filtered search, flexible payload indexing, quantization support, and both gRPC and REST APIs. Its limitations include a smaller community than Weaviate or Pinecone and fewer built-in integrations, and its cluster mode requires more manual configuration.

Milvus is open source under Apache 2.0 and is built from the ground up for billion-scale vector search. It uses a disaggregated storage-and-compute architecture with separate query nodes, data nodes, and index nodes, orchestrated by a coordinator layer. This design lets you scale ingestion and search workloads independently. Milvus supports a wide range of index types, including HNSW, IVF-Flat, IVF-PQ, IVF-SQ8, DiskANN, and notably GPU-accelerated indexes. The GPU indexes leverage NVIDIA RAPIDS for building and searching, achieving five to ten times throughput improvements on large-scale workloads. For datasets in the hundreds of millions to billions, Milvus can process thousands of queries per second at high recall. It is battle-tested at billion-scale deployments and offers strong consistency guarantees. Its main drawback is operational complexity, as the distributed architecture requires infrastructure expertise. The learning curve is steeper than Qdrant or Weaviate. Milvus is best for teams operating at genuine billion-vector scale and those comfortable managing distributed systems or willing to use the managed Zilliz Cloud.

Chroma is an open-source, Python-native vector database designed for simplicity and rapid prototyping. It uses SQLite to store metadata and a mapping between IDs and vectors, while HNSW via hnswlib handles the vector index. Both run in-process by default, making Chroma feel like an embedded database. The project has matured considerably, adding a client-server mode for multi-process access, persistent storage, token-based authentication, role-based access control, multi-tenancy, and observability hooks via OpenTelemetry. Chroma's API is dead simple with near-zero boilerplate. It supports automatic embedding generation from raw documents and rich metadata filtering. Its limitations are a single-node architecture without built-in sharding or replication, making it best suited for datasets in the low millions of vectors. The HNSW index is held in memory, so memory requirements grow linearly with collection size. Chroma is ideal for prototyping, development, small-to-medium production workloads, and educational projects.

Turbopuffer is a serverless vector database designed for cost-efficient large-scale search. It stores vectors on object storage like S3 and uses aggressive caching and custom query execution to serve low-latency queries without keeping entire indexes in memory. This makes its cost at large scale dramatically lower than in-memory alternatives, as storage pricing follows object-storage economics rather than RAM pricing. It supports hybrid search with BM25 and vector scoring in a single query and namespace-based multi-tenancy. But it is a newer entrant with a smaller ecosystem, and cold queries may be slower while caching mitigates that for active datasets. It is proprietary and managed only. Turbopuffer is best for cost-sensitive workloads with large vector counts and multi-tenant SaaS architectures.

LanceDB is an open-source, embedded vector database built on the Lance columnar data format. It runs in-process with zero-copy access to data on local disk or object storage. It has no server to manage, which makes it similar to SQLite for vectors. The Lance format supports versioned datasets with efficient appends and updates, making it well-suited for ML workflows where data evolves over time. It has native support for multi-modal data and automatic IVF-PQ index construction. However, its embedded architecture means no built-in multi-process concurrency, though Lance's MVCC allows concurrent readers. It is best for data science workflows, applications needing versioned vector datasets, edge deployments, and teams wanting to avoid managing a separate database server.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector data type and ANN search using both IVF and HNSW indexes. It leverages existing PostgreSQL infrastructure, giving you ACID transactions, joins with relational data, and a familiar SQL interface. You need no new infrastructure if you already use PostgreSQL. Its performance ceiling is lower than purpose-built vector databases, HNSW index builds can be slow and memory-intensive, and it is limited to single-node PostgreSQL performance characteristics. Still, services like Supabase and Neon add managed scaling.

chapters.title: Vector Search in Existing Databases
chapters.script: A dedicated vector database is not always the right answer. If your application already relies on a general-purpose database, adding vector search as an extension can reduce operational complexity, avoid data synchronization headaches, and keep your stack simpler. The trade-off is performance: purpose-built vector databases are optimized end-to-end for approximate nearest neighbor search, while bolt-on solutions inherit the performance characteristics and scaling constraints of their host systems. MongoDB Atlas Vector Search integrates vector search directly into the document model. You define a vector search index on an array field, and queries use an aggregation stage. Because vectors live alongside your documents, there is no ETL pipeline to keep in sync: when you update a document, the vector index updates with it. Atlas uses a proprietary ANN algorithm and supports pre-filtering on any indexed document field. Performance is competitive for datasets up to tens of millions of vectors, but it runs only on Atlas, not on self-hosted MongoDB. Elasticsearch added dense vector fields and HNSW-based ANN search in version 8.x. If you already use Elasticsearch for full-text search, adding vector search creates a natural hybrid retrieval pipeline where BM25 and vector scores can be combined in a single query. The advantage is one system for both sparse and dense retrieval. The limitation is resource overhead, as HNSW indexes are memory-intensive and the JVM-based architecture adds latency compared to native implementations. Supabase wraps pgvector with a managed PostgreSQL service, adding connection pooling and edge functions. Google's AlloyDB AI is a PostgreSQL-compatible managed database with a custom vector search engine that claims ten to one hundred times better ANN performance than standard pgvector, using Google's proprietary ScaNN algorithm. Both are compelling for teams committed to the PostgreSQL ecosystem. A decision framework: choose integrated vector search when your dataset is under roughly ten million vectors, you need ACID transactions spanning vector and relational data, operational simplicity outweighs raw search performance, and your team already operates the host database in production. Choose a dedicated vector database when scale exceeds tens of millions of vectors, query latency at high throughput is critical with sub-five millisecond p99, you need advanced features like multi-vector search or GPU acceleration, and vector search is a core product differentiator.

chapters.title: Indexing Strategies
chapters.script: When you decide which index to use, your scenario guides the choice. For fewer than one hundred thousand vectors, a flat or brute-force index gives exact results with low latency. For one hundred thousand to ten million vectors, HNSW is best, offering excellent recall-latency and fitting in memory. For ten million to one hundred million vectors, consider HNSW with quantization to reduce memory. For over one hundred million vectors, use IVF-PQ or HNSW combined with disk, where memory constraints dominate. For frequent updates, HNSW supports incremental insertion. For batch-only updates, you can use IVF-PQ and rebuild the index periodically. Building an HNSW index on ten million 768-dimensional vectors takes roughly thirty to sixty minutes on modern hardware. During construction, all vectors must be in memory, so plan for two to three times the final index size. HNSW supports incremental insertion with some quality degradation, while IVF requires full retraining of centroids if the distribution shifts significantly. After loading an HNSW index from disk, the first queries may be slow as graph nodes are loaded into cache, so pre-warm with representative queries.

chapters.title: Metadata Filtering
chapters.script: Real-world search queries almost always include metadata filters, like finding similar documents created in the last week by a certain author in a certain category. The interaction between vector search and metadata filtering is a critical architectural concern. There are three approaches. Post-filtering retrieves the top-K nearest vectors, then filters by metadata. This is simple but problematic: if ninety percent of vectors are filtered out, you need to retrieve ten times more candidates to get K results, which is wasteful and can miss relevant results entirely. Pre-filtering applies the metadata filter first, for example using a bitmap, then searches only within the filtered subset. This is more accurate but can be slow if the HNSW index was built over all vectors, not just the filtered subset. Integrated filtering, as used by Qdrant, evaluates metadata conditions during HNSW graph traversal, skipping nodes that do not match the filter. This avoids both the accuracy issues of post-filtering and the performance issues of pre-filtering. To support fast filtering, you create payload indexes on fields you filter by, such as keyword indexes for exact matches and datetime indexes for range queries.

chapters.title: Hybrid Search Architecture
chapters.script: Combining dense vector search with sparse lexical search, like BM25, consistently outperforms either approach alone. The architecture involves parallel retrieval, where you execute vector search and BM25 search simultaneously. Then you normalize scores from each source to a common scale. Next you fuse the results using reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted linear combination. Optionally, you apply a cross-encoder reranker to the fused results. In reciprocal rank fusion, each document gets a score based on its rank in each result list, combined using a constant k. You can weight the two sources with a parameter alpha that balances dense and sparse contributions. This hybrid pattern should be the default architecture for production RAG systems.

chapters.title: Scaling Patterns
chapters.script: As collections grow beyond single-node capacity, sharding becomes necessary. Hash-based sharding distributes vectors across nodes by a hash of the document ID. It gives a simple uniform distribution, but every query must fan out to all shards. Semantic sharding clusters vectors and assigns clusters to shards, so queries can be routed to relevant shards only, reducing fan-out. However, cluster boundaries can cause recall loss. Replication and consistency: vector databases typically offer eventual consistency for search results. A newly inserted vector may not appear immediately due to index rebuild lag, replication lag, or segment merge operations. For applications requiring immediate consistency, consider a two-tier approach: exact match on a hash or ID field with ACID guarantees, and ANN search for similarity. Cost optimization: vector search costs are dominated by memory for in-memory indexes or IOPS for disk-based indexes. Key strategies include quantization to reduce vector size, using Matryoshka truncation for lower dimensional retrieval followed by full dimension reranking, tiered storage that keeps hot data in memory and warm data on SSD, and index per partition that separates indexes by time range or tenant so you can delete entire indexes instead of individual vectors.

chapters.title: Operational Considerations
chapters.script: You need to monitor several critical metrics. Track recall at K by sampling ground truth periodically and measuring actual recall. Track query latency at the 50th, 95th, and 99th percentiles; tail latency often matters more than median. Monitor index build time for unexpected increases that might indicate a data distribution shift. Track memory utilization, because HNSW memory grows linearly with vector count. Track insert throughput for capacity planning. For backup and recovery, vector indexes are expensive to rebuild, so your backup strategy should include raw vectors and metadata for a full rebuild if needed, serialized index state for fast recovery, and regular snapshot testing to verify that backups can actually be restored. Migration between databases is a real concern for lock-in. Maintain the ability to export vectors and metadata in a standard format. The actual vectors are portable, but the index must be rebuilt in the target system. Budget for index build time during migration planning.

chapters.title: Multi-Vector Storage
chapters.script: Standard embedding models produce a single vector per document, compressing the entire semantic content into one point. ColBERT and similar late-interaction models take a different approach: they produce one vector per token, preserving fine-grained lexical-semantic information. This enables more precise matching, but introduces significant storage and search challenges. A two-hundred token passage as a single 768-dimensional float32 vector occupies three kilobytes. The same passage under ColBERT using 128-dimensional per-token vectors produces two hundred vectors at 512 bytes each, totalling one hundred kilobytes, a thirty-three times increase. At ten million passages, single-vector storage is about thirty gigabytes, while multi-vector storage balloons to one terabyte before indexing overhead. Compression is essential. ColBERTv2 introduced residual compression that quantizes vectors relative to their nearest centroid, reducing per-token storage to sixteen to thirty-two bytes. This brings the ten million passage figure down to fifty to eighty gigabytes, still larger than single-vector but manageable. The scoring mechanism, called MaxSim, computes the maximum similarity between each query token vector and all passage token vectors, then sums across query tokens. Naively this is computationally explosive. Practical implementations use a two-stage approach: first candidate generation using a standard ANN index over all token vectors to find passages with at least one highly similar token, then late interaction scoring only for candidates using decompressed token vectors. Dedicated ColBERT storage engines like RAGatouille and Vespa's native ColBERT support handle this complexity internally. Among general-purpose vector databases, Milvus supports multi-vector fields with per-document token-level storage and retrieval. Qdrant can store multi-vectors via its multi-vector feature. For most applications, evaluate whether the recall improvement from multi-vector representations justifies the storage and complexity cost. In domains with precise terminology like legal, medical, or technical documentation, token-level matching often provides meaningful gains. For general-purpose semantic search, a single high-quality embedding with hybrid BM25 retrieval typically gives a better complexity-to-quality ratio.

chapters.title: Runtime Internals
chapters.script: The tunable approximate index model hides the mechanics that decide production recall, latency, and cost. With HNSW, you build a layered proximity graph. Search greedily descends from a sparse top layer to dense lower layers, keeping a candidate list of size ef. A bigger ef means more of the graph is explored, giving higher recall and higher latency. The build-time parameter M, the number of edges per node, sets the memory and quality floor. The runtime lesson is that recall is a search-time dial, ef, on top of a build-time structure you cannot cheaply change later. With IVF and PQ, you first partition vectors into clusters. A query probes only nprobe nearest clusters, achieving sub-linear time. Product quantization compresses each vector into a few bytes so the index fits in RAM. The trade-off is that PQ introduces quantization error, so results are re-scored against full vectors in a re-ranking step. Nprobe is the recall and latency knob; PQ bits are the memory and recall knob. Filtered search combines a metadata filter with vector search, and there is a trap. Post-filtering searches then drops non-matching results, which can return zero results if the top-k all fail the filter. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set first, but can wreck HNSW graph connectivity. Production engines do filtering during traversal, and that runtime detail determines whether queries like find docs from 2024 similar to X actually work. Also, a vector index is bound to one embedding model and chunking configuration. Changing either invalidates every vector, requiring a full re-embed and re-index, not a migration you can do in place. The runtime needs a blue-green index swap, and for freshness, a strategy for incremental upserts versus periodic rebuilds. This is the operational cost the search and recommendations layer inherits whenever relevance is improved.

Elasticsearch added dense vector fields and HNSW-based ANN search in version 8.x. If you already use Elasticsearch for full-text search, adding vector search creates a natural hybrid retrieval pipeline where BM25 and vector scores can be combined in a single query. The advantage is one system for both sparse and dense retrieval. The limitation is resource overhead, as HNSW indexes are memory-intensive and the JVM-based architecture adds latency compared to native implementations. Supabase wraps pgvector with a managed PostgreSQL service, adding connection pooling and edge functions. Google's AlloyDB AI is a PostgreSQL-compatible managed database with a custom vector search engine that claims ten to one hundred times better ANN performance than standard pgvector, using Google's proprietary ScaNN algorithm. Both are compelling for teams committed to the PostgreSQL ecosystem. A decision framework: choose integrated vector search when your dataset is under roughly ten million vectors, you need ACID transactions spanning vector and relational data, operational simplicity outweighs raw search performance, and your team already operates the host database in production. Choose a dedicated vector database when scale exceeds tens of millions of vectors, query latency at high throughput is critical with sub-five millisecond p99, you need advanced features like multi-vector search or GPU acceleration, and vector search is a core product differentiator.

## Indexing Strategies

When you decide which index to use, your scenario guides the choice. For fewer than one hundred thousand vectors, a flat or brute-force index gives exact results with low latency. For one hundred thousand to ten million vectors, HNSW is best, offering excellent recall-latency and fitting in memory. For ten million to one hundred million vectors, consider HNSW with quantization to reduce memory. For over one hundred million vectors, use IVF-PQ or HNSW combined with disk, where memory constraints dominate. For frequent updates, HNSW supports incremental insertion. For batch-only updates, you can use IVF-PQ and rebuild the index periodically. Building an HNSW index on ten million 768-dimensional vectors takes roughly thirty to sixty minutes on modern hardware. During construction, all vectors must be in memory, so plan for two to three times the final index size. HNSW supports incremental insertion with some quality degradation, while IVF requires full retraining of centroids if the distribution shifts significantly. After loading an HNSW index from disk, the first queries may be slow as graph nodes are loaded into cache, so pre-warm with representative queries.

## Metadata Filtering

Real-world search queries almost always include metadata filters, like finding similar documents created in the last week by a certain author in a certain category. The interaction between vector search and metadata filtering is a critical architectural concern. There are three approaches. Post-filtering retrieves the top-K nearest vectors, then filters by metadata. This is simple but problematic: if ninety percent of vectors are filtered out, you need to retrieve ten times more candidates to get K results, which is wasteful and can miss relevant results entirely. Pre-filtering applies the metadata filter first, for example using a bitmap, then searches only within the filtered subset. This is more accurate but can be slow if the HNSW index was built over all vectors, not just the filtered subset. Integrated filtering, as used by Qdrant, evaluates metadata conditions during HNSW graph traversal, skipping nodes that do not match the filter. This avoids both the accuracy issues of post-filtering and the performance issues of pre-filtering. To support fast filtering, you create payload indexes on fields you filter by, such as keyword indexes for exact matches and datetime indexes for range queries.

## Hybrid Search Architecture

Combining dense vector search with sparse lexical search, like BM25, consistently outperforms either approach alone. The architecture involves parallel retrieval, where you execute vector search and BM25 search simultaneously. Then you normalize scores from each source to a common scale. Next you fuse the results using reciprocal rank fusion or a weighted linear combination. Optionally, you apply a cross-encoder reranker to the fused results. In reciprocal rank fusion, each document gets a score based on its rank in each result list, combined using a constant k. You can weight the two sources with a parameter alpha that balances dense and sparse contributions. This hybrid pattern should be the default architecture for production RAG systems.

## Scaling Patterns

As collections grow beyond single-node capacity, sharding becomes necessary. Hash-based sharding distributes vectors across nodes by a hash of the document ID. It gives a simple uniform distribution, but every query must fan out to all shards. Semantic sharding clusters vectors and assigns clusters to shards, so queries can be routed to relevant shards only, reducing fan-out. However, cluster boundaries can cause recall loss. Replication and consistency: vector databases typically offer eventual consistency for search results. A newly inserted vector may not appear immediately due to index rebuild lag, replication lag, or segment merge operations. For applications requiring immediate consistency, consider a two-tier approach: exact match on a hash or ID field with ACID guarantees, and ANN search for similarity. Cost optimization: vector search costs are dominated by memory for in-memory indexes or IOPS for disk-based indexes. Key strategies include quantization to reduce vector size, using Matryoshka truncation for lower dimensional retrieval followed by full dimension reranking, tiered storage that keeps hot data in memory and warm data on SSD, and index per partition that separates indexes by time range or tenant so you can delete entire indexes instead of individual vectors.

## Operational Considerations

You need to monitor several critical metrics. Track recall at K by sampling ground truth periodically and measuring actual recall. Track query latency at the 50th, 95th, and 99th percentiles; tail latency often matters more than median. Monitor index build time for unexpected increases that might indicate a data distribution shift. Track memory utilization, because HNSW memory grows linearly with vector count. Track insert throughput for capacity planning. For backup and recovery, vector indexes are expensive to rebuild, so your backup strategy should include raw vectors and metadata for a full rebuild if needed, serialized index state for fast recovery, and regular snapshot testing to verify that backups can actually be restored. Migration between databases is a real concern for lock-in. Maintain the ability to export vectors and metadata in a standard format. The actual vectors are portable, but the index must be rebuilt in the target system. Budget for index build time during migration planning.

## Multi-Vector Storage

Standard embedding models produce a single vector per document, compressing the entire semantic content into one point. ColBERT and similar late-interaction models take a different approach: they produce one vector per token, preserving fine-grained lexical-semantic information. This enables more precise matching, but introduces significant storage and search challenges. A two-hundred token passage as a single 768-dimensional float32 vector occupies three kilobytes. The same passage under ColBERT using 128-dimensional per-token vectors produces two hundred vectors at 512 bytes each, totalling one hundred kilobytes, a thirty-three times increase. At ten million passages, single-vector storage is about thirty gigabytes, while multi-vector storage balloons to one terabyte before indexing overhead. Compression is essential. ColBERTv2 introduced residual compression that quantizes vectors relative to their nearest centroid, reducing per-token storage to sixteen to thirty-two bytes. This brings the ten million passage figure down to fifty to eighty gigabytes, still larger than single-vector but manageable. The scoring mechanism, called MaxSim, computes the maximum similarity between each query token vector and all passage token vectors, then sums across query tokens. Naively this is computationally explosive. Practical implementations use a two-stage approach: first candidate generation using a standard ANN index over all token vectors to find passages with at least one highly similar token, then late interaction scoring only for candidates using decompressed token vectors. Dedicated ColBERT storage engines like RAGatouille and Vespa's native ColBERT support handle this complexity internally. Among general-purpose vector databases, Milvus supports multi-vector fields with per-document token-level storage and retrieval. Qdrant can store multi-vectors via its multi-vector feature. For most applications, evaluate whether the recall improvement from multi-vector representations justifies the storage and complexity cost. In domains with precise terminology like legal, medical, or technical documentation, token-level matching often provides meaningful gains. For general-purpose semantic search, a single high-quality embedding with hybrid BM25 retrieval typically gives a better complexity-to-quality ratio.

## Runtime Internals

The tunable approximate index model hides the mechanics that decide production recall, latency, and cost. With HNSW, you build a layered proximity graph. Search greedily descends from a sparse top layer to dense lower layers, keeping a candidate list of size ef. A bigger ef means more of the graph is explored, giving higher recall and higher latency. The build-time parameter M, the number of edges per node, sets the memory and quality floor. The runtime lesson is that recall is a search-time dial, ef, on top of a build-time structure you cannot cheaply change later. With IVF and PQ, you first partition vectors into clusters. A query probes only nprobe nearest clusters, achieving sub-linear time. Product quantization compresses each vector into a few bytes so the index fits in RAM. The trade-off is that PQ introduces quantization error, so results are re-scored against full vectors in a re-ranking step. Nprobe is the recall and latency knob; PQ bits are the memory and recall knob. Filtered search combines a metadata filter with vector search, and there is a trap. Post-filtering searches then drops non-matching results, which can return zero results if the top-k all fail the filter. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set first, but can wreck HNSW graph connectivity. Production engines do filtering during traversal, and that runtime detail determines whether queries like find docs from 2024 similar to X actually work. Also, a vector index is bound to one embedding model and chunking configuration. Changing either invalidates every vector, requiring a full re-embed and re-index, not a migration you can do in place. The runtime needs a blue-green index swap, and for freshness, a strategy for incremental upserts versus periodic rebuilds. This is the operational cost the search and recommendations layer inherits whenever relevance is improved.
